opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here.

Twelve years is a nice window, because it takes us back to roughly 2012, and that's really the watershed. That's when AlexNet won the ImageNet competition and showed that deep neural networks, trained on large amounts of data with GPUs, could dramatically outperform the hand-engineered features we'd all been using in computer vision. That surprised a lot of us. I remember people in the field being skeptical, and within about two years almost everyone had switched over.

For robotics, that mattered enormously, because perception had always been one of our biggest bottlenecks. Suddenly robots could recognize objects and segment scenes far more reliably. In my lab we applied those ideas to grasping. We built a system called Dex-Net that trained on millions of synthetic examples generated in simulation, and it could pick up objects it had never seen before with quite high reliability. That kind of work helped launch what's now a real industry in warehouse picking and e-commerce fulfillment.

The second big breakthrough, of course, is the transformer architecture, and then large language models. ChatGPT in late 2022 was a moment where the public suddenly saw what these systems could do. I think even researchers were surprised by how far you could get with scale and next-token prediction. And now we're seeing vision-language-action models, where people try to bring that same recipe into robotics, plus diffusion policies and other generative approaches for learning robot behaviors from demonstrations.

But I want to add a note of caution, because there's a lot of hype right now, especially around humanoids. Language models had the benefit of an enormous amount of text on the internet. Robotics doesn't have that. If you add up all the data we have of robots actually manipulating things, it's tiny by comparison. I've estimated it would take something like a hundred thousand years of robot experience to match the amount of text these language models are trained on. So there's a huge data gap.

This connects to what's called Moravec's paradox: the things that are easy for humans, like picking up a glass or folding a towel, are actually very hard for robots, while things we find hard, like chess or calculus, have turned out to be relatively easy for computers. That paradox is still very much with us.

So I'd say the breakthroughs have been real and profound, in perception especially, and in language. But in physical manipulation, we're making steady progress rather than the kind of sudden leap some people are predicting. I think we'll get there through a combination of approaches: learning from data, yes, but also good old-fashioned engineering, physics, and models. Not one or the other.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I've been working on robots since the mid-1980s, so twelve years is a relatively short window for me, but it happens to contain some of the most dramatic changes I've ever witnessed.

The first thing I'd point to is deep learning for perception. Around 2012, with AlexNet and the ImageNet results, we suddenly had computer vision that actually worked. For decades, getting a robot to recognize an object in a cluttered scene was a research project unto itself. Almost overnight that became something you could more or less take off the shelf. For robotics that was enormous, because perception had always been one of the big bottlenecks.

The second is what happened in simulation and data. In my own lab, with the Dex-Net project, we started generating millions of synthetic grasps using physics and geometry, and training networks on that rather than on hand-collected examples. The idea that you could learn robust behavior largely from simulated data and have it transfer to a real robot was a real shift. It changed how people thought about collecting experience for robots.

Third, obviously, is the large language models. I'll be honest, I did not predict that. The fact that you can now talk to a system in natural language and have it reason about a task, break it into steps, even write code to control a robot, that's a qualitatively new capability. It's opened up the idea of robots that can take high-level instructions rather than being painstakingly programmed.

And fourth, I'd say the convergence of all these into what people are calling foundation models for robotics, these vision-language-action models. There's a lot of excitement, and a lot of money flowing in, and I think some of it is justified.

But I want to add a note of caution, because I think it's important. Robotics is still hard. There's something I've been calling the hundred-thousand-year data gap. Language models trained on essentially the entire written output of humanity, trillions of words. The amount of robot manipulation data we have is minuscule by comparison. And unlike text, you can't just scrape it off the internet, you have to go out and physically collect it, or simulate it, and simulation of contact and deformable objects is still very imperfect.

So I think of this as a classic Moravec's paradox situation. The things that are hard for humans, like playing chess or passing the bar exam, turn out to be comparatively easy for machines. The things a two-year-old does effortlessly, like picking up a sock and folding it, remain genuinely difficult. We've made real progress on the first category in the past twelve years. On the second, we've made progress too, but I'd say it's more incremental than the headlines suggest.

So I'm very excited, but I'd call myself a cautious optimist. The breakthroughs are real. The hype is also real, and I think separating the two is one of the most important things we can do right now.

astra-6.text:
I’d point to deep learning as the biggest breakthrough in AI over that period. The ability to learn useful patterns from large amounts of data has transformed computer vision, speech recognition, and, more recently, language. For robotics, vision is particularly important: a robot needs to make sense of what’s around it before it can do anything useful.

But there’s a gap between recognising something in an image and physically interacting with it. If you want to pick up an object, you have to work out where to grasp it, how much force to apply, and what to do if it slips. Small errors in perception can have real consequences when you make contact with the world.

One development I’m particularly excited about is using learning to improve those physical skills. We can collect examples of grasps, learn from successes and failures, and use simulation to explore many more possibilities than we could test with a single robot. And cloud robotics—the idea that robots can share data and computation over a network—creates an opportunity for experience on one robot to benefit others.

The challenge is reliability. A demonstration that works once is exciting, but a robot that can work consistently across unfamiliar objects and conditions is a much higher bar. We’ve made substantial progress, but that distinction is essential to understanding where robotics stands.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d point to deep learning as the biggest breakthrough in AI over that period, particularly its impact on computer vision. For robotics, being able to interpret an image—to recognize objects and estimate where they are—is enormously important. And we’ve made remarkable progress there.

But there’s a gap between recognizing something and interacting with it. You can look at a coffee cup and identify it with high confidence, but picking it up requires understanding its geometry, choosing where to grasp it, and dealing with what happens when your fingers make contact. Those are different problems, and the physical world is full of uncertainty.

One development I find especially exciting is using learning together with models of the physics. We can generate examples in simulation, use them to learn how to grasp objects, and then test those grasps on a real robot. That opens up ways to handle objects the robot hasn’t encountered before.

So I’d say the major breakthrough is our ability to learn from data, with vision as the clearest success. In robotics, we’re beginning to translate that into reliable action. But the pace is different: software can make millions of predictions very quickly, while a robot has to move, make contact, and recover when something goes wrong. That makes progress in the physical world a much harder undertaking.
